Which is worse: malice or incompetence? Why?
Malice. You can avoid an incompetent person, but a malicious person can't be avoided.

Malice. Aside from the ethical implications, and the fact that you can probably trust an incompetent person to not deliberately fuck you up or over to reflect their own interests, it is usually much easier to handle the results of incompetence than a deliberate and targeted exercise in malice. Furthermore, incompetence can often be addressed with additional training, or in some cases a transfer to other duties.

Of course, these are generalizations, but this is a broad question to a situation that is subject to many specific permutations, and as such you can't really get into every possible scenario.
Sufficiently advanced malice is indistinguishable from incompetence.
At least malicious people can be manipulated to serve their self-interests. That may be a way to distinguish advanced malice from incompetence, in situations complex enough to allow it.

Incompetence of course. You rarely see it coming, and you can't really hold anyone accountable because it's not like it was their fault.

Malice OTOH is expected and predictable, so you can plan for it. And if you don't plan for it then you're incompetent.
Malice. Incompetence is not always going to result in bad things, but malice will.
Your smart home is no longer supported

Shutting down Revolv does not mean that Nest is ceasing to support its products, leaving them vulnerable to bugs and other unpatched issues. It means that the $300 devices and accompanying apps will stop working completely.

This is one reason why I believe that automatic updates are, in general, a bad thing. Contrary to the endless mantra, it's very clear that companies do not have your interests in mind whatsoever with them. In many ways it's basically a back door.

Of course, people think I'm a lunatic and/or just plain stupid regarding computers, or I "don't understand" why people "should" upgrade. Until stuff like this starts becoming more common. And it almost certainly will, even if the courts step in.

I believe that automatic updates are, in general, a bad thing.

Automatic updates are not per se a bad thing. Most people don't upgrade their router/TV/phone/whatever firmware every time there is a security hole. This allows huge botnets rented out to send spam and do ddos attacks. Most people would do better with automatic updates but it should be optional.

Automatic updates are not per se a bad thing.

In theory, they are a very good thing. In practice, under the supervision of entities that have interests that may go directly against users and owners of the involved equipment, they are a massive, gaping hole that allows for many bad things, and that is made significantly worse when you are forced to accept them. That is, unless you essentially sabotage the device, which has consequences in and of itself.

There are a few pieces of software where I would generally trust updates to at least not be deliberately against my interests, particularly many Linux distributions. However, I am suspicious at best of most others, and even the "good" ones can end up debilitating the system involved, such as Firefox's tendency to remove features (and in some cases try to replace them with something that will make Mozilla money).

I am aware automatic updates are a two sided blade and could be abused. But IMO having most of the devices online, with known vulnerabilities is the worse of two evils.

And checking checksums is worth nothing if you get the checksum from the same source as the file to check. Whoever can intercept your download can also replace the checksum.

And don't get me started on Mozilla removing features in Firefox.
